title: File I/O
description: Master reading from and writing to files in C# using the File class, StreamReader, StreamWriter, and async I/O patterns for real-world applications.

data.text: **File I/O (Input/Output)** is how your programs communicate with the file system. Every time your app saves a user's progress, exports a report, or loads a configuration file, it uses file I/O. C# provides several approaches ranging from simple one-liners to efficient streaming for large files.

File I/O stands for **Input/Output** — it describes any operation where a program reads data from an external source (input) or writes data to an external destination (output). In C#, that external destination is typically the file system on disk. Without file I/O, your program would lose everything when it closes, because variables and objects only exist in memory (RAM) while the program runs.

data.text: The File Class — Simple Read and Write

The `System.IO.File` class provides static methods that are perfect for small to medium-sized files. These methods are the simplest to use because you don't need to create or manage any objects. They load the entire file into memory at once, which is convenient but means they're not ideal for very large files.

data.title: Read All Text
data.content: Use ReadAllText when you need the entire file as a single string, such as a short configuration file or a poem.

data.text: Reading Line by Line with ReadAllLines

data.title: Read All Lines
data.content: Use ReadAllLines when you want to process each line individually, such as parsing a CSV or log file.

data.title: Write and Append
data.content: WriteAllText overwrites the file, while AppendAllText adds to the end. WriteAllLines creates a fresh file with multiple lines.

data.text: The `File` class methods load the entire file into memory at once. For large files — such as a 500 MB log file or a multi-gigabyte dataset — this can exhaust available memory and slow down or even crash your program. **Streams** solve this by reading and writing data incrementally, one piece at a time, keeping memory usage constant regardless of file size.

data.text: StreamReader — Reading Line by Line Efficiently

`StreamReader` reads data character by character or line by line from a file. It is wrapped in a `using` statement so the file handle is automatically closed when reading is complete — even if an error occurs partway through.

data.title: StreamReader for Large Files
data.content: StreamReader is ideal when you need to process one line at a time without loading the whole file into memory.

data.title: StreamWriter for Bulk Writes
data.content: StreamWriter buffers writes for efficiency. Call Flush or Close when done to ensure all data reaches the disk.

data.text: Real applications rarely deal with a single flat file. They organize files into directories, need to build paths dynamically, and must work on Windows, Mac, and Linux. The `System.IO.Path` and `System.IO.Directory` classes handle this cross-platform complexity for you.

data.title: Directory and Path Operations
data.content: Create directories, build paths safely, and enumerate files using Directory and Path helpers.

data.title: Cross-Platform Path Safety
data.text: Always use Path.Combine() instead of string concatenation for paths. Windows uses backslashes (\), while macOS and Linux use forward slashes (/). Path.Combine handles the correct separator automatically. Similarly, use Environment.NewLine for line breaks so your app works on every OS.

For applications with user interfaces or web servers, blocking the main thread with file operations makes the app feel sluggish. **Async file I/O** uses the Task-based Asynchronous Pattern (TAP) to keep your application responsive. The `await` keyword lets the thread serve other work while the file operation completes.

data.title: Async File Read and Write
data.content: Use ReadAllTextAsync and WriteAllTextAsync for non-blocking file operations.

data.title: Build a Simple Todo File Manager
data.description: Create a console app that manages a todo list stored in a text file. Each todo is one line. The app should add, list, and delete todos.
steps: Create a text file named todos.txt with a few sample items.
Write a method AddTodo(string task) that appends a new task to the file.
Write a method ListTodos() that reads all lines and displays them with numbers.
Write a method DeleteTodo(int number) that removes the task at the given line number.
Wrap all file operations in try/catch blocks and print friendly error messages.
Call each method from Main() to verify the behavior.
data.expectedOutcome: A working todo manager that persists tasks to disk between runs, with clear user prompts and error handling.

items.question: What is the difference between File.ReadAllText and StreamReader?
items.answer: ReadAllText loads the entire file into memory at once and returns a single string. StreamReader reads incrementally (one line or one character at a time), using far less memory for large files.

items.question: Do I need to call Close() on streams?
items.answer: No, if you wrap the stream in a using statement, the Dispose() method (which Close() calls internally) is invoked automatically when the block ends.

items.question: What exceptions can file I/O throw?
items.answer: Common exceptions include FileNotFoundException, DirectoryNotFoundException, UnauthorizedAccessException, IOException, and PathTooLongException. Always use try/catch around file operations in production code.

items.question: When should I use async file I/O?
items.answer: Use async I/O for UI applications, ASP.NET web servers, or anywhere blocking the main thread would degrade user experience. For console scripts that run quickly, synchronous I/O is fine.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: File.ReadAllText and ReadAllLines load whole files into memory
WriteAllText overwrites; AppendAllText adds to the end
using ensures streams are disposed correctly
data.takeaway: File I/O enables data persistence. Choose the right tool: simple File methods for small files, streams for large ones, and async for responsive apps.
